ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is a life‑threatening state in children 6‑59 months defined by very low MUAC, low weight‑for‑height Z‑score, or bilateral oedema. Prompt identification, treatment of infection and nutritional rehabilitation are essential.

sections.p: SAM is diagnosed when any of the following are present: MUAC <115 mm, weight‑for‑height Z‑score <‑3, or bilateral pitting oedema. These criteria are age‑specific for children 6‑59 months.
b: Bilateral pitting oedema is a danger sign regardless of MUAC

sections.p: WHO classifies SAM as uncomplicated or complicated. Complicated SAM has any medical complication (infection, shock, severe dehydration, severe anaemia) or inability to eat.
b: Uncomplicated: stable, can be managed outpatient
Complicated: needs inpatient care, IV antibiotics, and close monitoring

sections.p: SAM results from inadequate intake, increased needs, or disease‑related losses. In low‑resource settings infections are common precipitants.
b: Chronic infections: HIV, TB, malaria, diarrhoea
Congenital or cardiac disease increasing metabolic demand

sections.p: Children appear thin, may have oedema, irritability, lethargy, and are prone to infections. Growth measurements are markedly below norms.
b: Visible wasting of limbs and abdomen

sections.p: Basic labs guide treatment and identify complications. When a test is unavailable, clinical judgment and WHO guidelines direct care.

t.b: Is the child severely wasted? <115 mm confirms SAM
Quantifies severity of wasting; <‑3 confirms SAM
Detects anaemia, leukocytosis; anaemia <7 g/dL may need transfusion
Identifies hypoglycaemia; <2.5 mmol/L requires immediate dextrose
Detects re‑feeding syndrome; low K or phosphate signals need cautious feeding
Establishes HIV status; positive guides antiretroviral and prophylactic decisions
Looks for pneumonia or TB; infiltrates guide antibiotic choice

sections.p: Complications can rapidly become fatal; early recognition saves lives.
Treat infection first, then start therapeutic feeding while monitoring for re‑feeding complications.
b: IV antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin + gentamicin) for all complicated SAM
Start ready‑to‑use therapeutic food (RUTF) or F‑75/F‑100 formulas as per protocol
Micronutrient supplementation: vitamin A, zinc, folic acid

sections.p: After stabilization, transition to outpatient therapeutic feeding with regular growth monitoring and immunisation updates.
b: Screen for HIV, TB, and other chronic conditions

sections.p: Conditions that may look similar but have different management.
b: Kwashiorkor (edematous malnutrition, often with normal MUAC)

sections.p: Some measurements may appear normal despite severe disease.
b: MUAC can be falsely high in oedematous children; always assess for oedema
Weight may be maintained by fluid overload, masking wasting

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent vomiting or inability to drink
Signs of shock (cold extremities, rapid weak pulse)

faq.q: Why is MUAC preferred for community screening?
faq.a: It is quick, does not require scales, and predicts mortality better than weight alone.

faq.q: Can a child with oedema be considered well‑nourished?
faq.a: No; bilateral pitting oedema is a danger sign of SAM regardless of MUAC or weight.

faq.q: When are antibiotics indicated in SAM?
faq.a: In any child with complicated SAM, or with any sign of infection, because immune function is severely impaired.

exam: List the WHO diagnostic criteria for severe acute malnutrition in a 12‑month‑old child.

Describe the first three steps in managing a child with SAM who presents with hypoglycaemia.
